extracted.intended_audience: journalists and reporters producing audio scripts and digital news stories (NPR staff and similar newsrooms)
extracted.subtask_short: news attribution for audio and digital reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Practical newsroom guidance on when, how, and why to attribute information in audio scripts and digital stories, including verb choice, placement, verification, and sourcing rules. Emphasizes both ethical standards and stylistic choices for different media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribution simply means revealing where you got the facts in your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The source can be a person you interviewed, a public institution or commercial enterprise putting out a statement, a published report or study, or another news outlet with an exclusive report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons to attribute (why do it?)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accountability — show where information comes from so it doesn't seem invented. Transparency — explain how you came by a fact because reliability often depends on the source. Reproducibility — let readers seek out the source independently. Credit — attribute to signal appreciation and build relationships. Self-Protection — directs questions about a fact to the source, although reporters still must ensure source credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: What needs attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Here are categories of information that generally require attribution: Quotes; New facts; Accusations/allegations; Disputed or controversial information; Anything that's not common knowledge; Anything sweeping in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not everything needs attribution — incontrovertible facts (e.g., 'The U.S.-Mexico border is 1,952 miles long') can stand by themselves. But new or contestable figures and claims should have explicit sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify attribution / Be a detective
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribution alone is not enough. You, the reporter, are responsible for making sure the source knows what they are talking about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check figures (do the math), consider implications, ask probing questions like 'How do you know that?' and ensure the source isn't misinformed. A source can be wrong without intending to mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to write attributions (structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most attributions contain a verb like 'said' or a preposition like 'according to,' paired with a source identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “British Prime Minister Rishi Sunak said in a statement …”; “One new study in the American Journal of Public Health found …”; “… according to the Japan Meteorological Agency.” Note that sometimes the source is technically a statement or document rather than the person named.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribution usually goes at the beginning or end of a sentence or clause; placement may differ by medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In digital pieces attribution usually goes after the fact because the fact is more important there. Audio stories, which are often personality-driven, often start with the attribution since the speaker may be more important than the fact. Vary placement for clarity or variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb choice matters (tone and distancing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The verbs used in attribution have shades of meaning: some cast doubt, others suggest certitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Says'/'said' is non-judgmental and conversational (good for audio). 'Maintain' or 'argue' signal distancing. 'Claim' is a strong word — use only when you are downright suspicious and have demonstrable reason to doubt the source. When you believe something but can't prove it, use 'suggests' or 'indicates.' Examples from the text: CDC says...; Police maintain...; The bank robbers claimed...; A new study suggests...; The spokesperson indicated...

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid amorphous groups like 'experts' or 'analysts'
rubrics_metrics.description: When attributing to people, avoid using amorphous groups like 'experts' or 'analysts' because they can imply a broader consensus than exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you spoke to a small number, attribute individually or use a narrower descriptor (e.g., 'economists who've studied universal basic income say …').

rubrics_metrics.name: Name your sources / anonymous sourcing policy
rubrics_metrics.description: NPR prefers to name the people we get our information from and has strict rules about anonymous sourcing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the NPR Ethics Handbook on anonymous sourcing; name sources whenever possible, and use anonymity only according to the organization's rules and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite other media sparingly and credit explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: NPR tries to do its own reporting but will quote other reliable news outlets when they have a scoop and their sourcing seems solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague terms like 'reportedly.' Instead give explicit credit to the outlet that broke the story when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt attribution to medium (text vs audio) and balance detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed attribution mattered more in print than radio historically, but online audio scripts also persist and are searchable; however, adding too many attributions can make broadcast scripts clunky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In broadcast, focus on the newest or most controversial facts for explicit attribution to avoid clutter, but ensure all facts are checked with the same rigor as those attributed in digital pieces. Don't rely on secondhand information.
